items.question: How do you understand the experience of learning to do research during a PhD?
items.object: The PhD experience and the qualities needed to make research progress
items.answer:
The PhD is a very, very interesting time. It's interesting because I think you sort of come in with grand ideas and passion to do things. Then the first one or two years is literally you just reorienting yourself, and trying to figure out, sort of, gain a foothold into this whole research community, and trying to figure out how do you even do research? How do you write papers, all that, right?

One of the things that I really had to learn from scratch was just being proactive. You know, figuring out things on your own, being independent. I think I had all these qualities before, but I cannot emphasize how important that is when you're a PhD student and you sort of want to make progress or figure out your niche, right? I think those things are probably far more important than your IQ level or how smart you are and things like that.

So I think the PhD was a really rewarding experience. Overall it was great. I feel like the PhD gives you the time and space to really go deep on something that, unfortunately, you don't get after.

items.question: What drew you toward language grounding during your PhD?
items.object: His attraction to reinforcement learning and language grounding
items.answer:
I started off working on some core NLP tasks, things like information extraction and some kind of sentiment analysis, all that. But then very quickly I figured out my love for RL was still there. And this was actually because of—I would credit my undergrad prof here, Professor Ravindra, and he's still at IIT Madras. He taught this RL course which was so interesting, so fascinating. So I kept thinking about RL, right?

And so, I would say from the third year onwards, most of my PhD was devoted to this language grounding area, where you're basically using reinforcement learning to teach these systems how to understand language. Just like how you're doing or I'm doing as humans.

items.question: What kind of AI research do you feel most drawn to?
items.object: His preferred style of AI research
items.answer: The one guiding sort of principle I always try to strive for is to try and basically push the envelope and define new areas. And there's several different kinds of research you can do, right? You can develop new models that solve really challenging tasks. You can be really good at empirical analysis and have really nice papers that showcase the different strengths and weaknesses. But I feel like the place that I'm most comfortable is just trying to imagine one or two steps into the future and try to bring that and close the gap between what we're seeing now and that. So I think most of the things that you just talked about have that flavor. I wouldn't say I'm specifically oriented towards methods or benchmarking. I think all of these are necessary.

items.question: How did you experience OpenAI as a research environment when you worked there?
items.object: OpenAI’s research environment during Karthik Narasimhan’s time there
items.answer: Yeah, it was super fun. I always tell people, OpenAI back then, it was a nonprofit, right? But it was basically just, like, a very well-funded research lab. And the thing that I started off doing there, working with folks like Ilya and Igor, was actually looking at this problem of multi-agent coordination and communication. So GPT was actually something that Alec was really pushing on, and I sort of helped him. But I think there were just so many different ideas. It was like a cauldron of this multi-agent stuff, the RLs, the robotic stuff, and then the Dota stuff came along. So it was a really fun time. I think the people there were so warm, yet, like, super smart. We were able to talk about things ranging from low-level details to AGI and philosophical discussions and all that. items.question: What excited you about transformer pre-training when you started as a professor?
items.object: Transformer pre-training as an early research direction
items.answer: When I started off, there was a time of BERT, right? So BERT came out right after GPT. Then they took the bidirectional side of things. I think it was pretty exciting even back then, because it was kind of clear that using a transformer, you can go way further than LSTM, which were the state of the art back then, right? So I think there was a whole line of looking at how pre-training is evolving. That was when the whole pre-training thing evolved, right? Basically, you train it on a bunch of raw text, and then you have these parameters that are initialized in such a nice way. So I think at that point, I would roughly categorize my interest as, like, okay, figure out what's happening with pre-training. How can this apply broadly, not just to NLP?

items.question: What did you see as missing from classical reinforcement learning for practical applications?
items.object: The gap between classical reinforcement learning theory and practical training
items.answer: I was trying to figure out what is missing in RL and what are things that can make it more practical, right? Because if you actually look at the formalization of RL in the classic Sutton and Barto, it's great as a formalism in the theoretical sense. But a lot of things are not really practical, right? So theoretically, yes, you will converge to the optimal policy, blah, blah, blah. But in reality, that's so far from what you wanna do, right? And in fact, for critical applications like training a robot, you can't have it destroy itself thousands of times. That was kind of the motivation towards what can you do to train these models safely using RL, POLCO, and all of that.

items.question: What purpose do you find most interesting for an AI benchmark?
items.object: AI benchmarks as a way to encourage work on useful capabilities
items.answer: So I think a benchmark can serve multiple purposes, and it's important to distinguish those purposes, I think. On the one hand, there is the quantitative aspect of it where you sort of have a leaderboard and you could be like, "Oh, this model is number three, and this model is number two, and there's the gap of two points between them." I think that's useful as a ranking mechanism. There's a different purpose, right? The other purpose is also just to showcase a sort of task or a capability which is useful, and you want the model to get better at that, right? Any model. It doesn't matter which model. You just want to climb to 100%, right? So I feel like people also look at benchmarks in one of these two angles. To me, the more interesting angle is the second one, which is, you feel like there's some capability that the model could have, but it's probably maybe currently lacking. Maybe it's not all the way there, but you want to push the community towards improving on that, right? And so I try to go for those kind of tasks where it seems like, "Hey, why are we not working on this thing?" So a benchmark is a good way to sort of kickstart more community involvement there.

items.question: How do you judge when improvements on an AI benchmark are worth pursuing?
items.object: Interpreting improvements on AI benchmark leaderboards
items.answer: I think the ranking part is useful, right? Obviously, it's useful when you sort of benchmark your model against your competitor's model or somebody else's model. But beyond a certain point, I don't think you wanna over-rotate on those results, right? Like, if you're at 20% and then you go up to, like, 80%, that's great. That's a very clear signal. But if everyone's at 80% and you're climbing to 81 and 82, I mean, at that point, all benchmarks get saturated, all benchmarks have issues. So at that point, it's probably worth your time to actually look at the next thing, right? I think those are some principles in hindsight that I feel like they're worth thinking about.

items.question: How do you see the contribution of SWE-bench and the SWE-agent harness to progress on realistic software engineering tasks?
items.object: SWE-bench and the SWE-agent harness
items.answer:
I think SWE-bench and the SWE-agent harness were important in surfacing some of these things, right? Like, what's missing? You have these strong models. They're clearly capable of writing good code. They're clearly capable of performing RAG. They're clearly capable of navigating file structures and telling you which file to click on, all that. So I think the thing that just got highlighted was, okay, there are two gaps to solve.

One was having the right harness. We call them coding agent harnesses now. Basically giving them the right tools, the right ACI in some sense, like agent computer interface. And second of all is just training on more data that's specific for these coding tasks, right? Which is not just code, but also the types of edits you wanna make and the file navigation, all that.

And I think we've seen both of them happen, right? So a lot of people have tried out different harnesses, like SWE-agent is one, Open Hands. Other people have tried out different things, like A+. So it's great. We've tried out very different things. We've learned lessons. And then the model building companies have taken this to heart as well. And they train the models on better data, specifically geared towards software engineering tasks, and made them stronger there.

So in that sense, I would say it's exactly the thing that SWE-bench was aiming to do, right? Like, make us move from being like, "Okay, generate one function piece of code and then test it," to actually solving more realistic SWE tasks. So I think having that sort of principle in mind is useful for any new benchmarks you use going forward.

items.question: What do you find most exciting about the user simulation in Tau Bench?
items.object: User simulation in Tau Bench and its implications for AI evaluation
items.answer:
I think one of the most exciting things to take from the whole Tau Bench paper is the fact that we can just simulate users really well now, right? And I know it seems like a small thing, and user simulation is not a new thing. People have worked on it for decades. But the fact that you can do it with such high fidelity has great implications. Because if you think about how AI systems are gonna be used in the future, they're not gonna be in isolation. There's always gonna be a human interacting with the systems at some level, right?

This was always something we put off before because the model was just not good enough. You're like, “Oh, why are you talking about human-AI interaction when the AI can't even do two things,” right? But I think we're in this phase now where that's gonna be critical, and that just means that all your evals are not just going to be like, “Hey, I collected a data set, and it's a static data set, and I just run the model through it.” We have to have more dynamic evals.

And I think that's where these kind of simulations are, where you're basically having dynamic interactions between different models. It can be as simple as a user simulator, or it could be cooperative or competitive multi-agent systems and all that. So there's this whole spectrum where you can slide the slider. But I think that's definitely the way that we're gonna go in the future, right? And in the future we'll also have humans ideally interacting with the systems live, right? And having that be part of the eval. But that requires a different skill.

items.question: How do you think about continual learning as a research problem for AI agents?
items.object: Continual learning for AI agents
items.answer:
I think the continual learning part is almost like a problem that needs to be solved. There's not really a specific algorithm or anything. I mean, continual learning, by the way, the problem space has existed for a few years now, right? But I think it's obvious why it needs to be solved. Because you can't be prompting the agent to do something and then expect it to just continue to work in the same way forever. Like, you want it to be dynamic. You want it to learn from its mistakes.

So I think this is a space where maybe all the chatter is just because it has to be solved. It's very, very obvious. Even take, for example, customer service. You want these agents to learn and become better over time, right? This is actually something that Sierra's advantage is: you can actually do that with the data and all that.

So I think it's an important thing. It's something everyone wants to solve. I don't think there's a specific algorithm that's the winner right now, or a specific method yet. But I suspect we'll see more of these crop up.

items.question: What do you see as the main challenge in applying reinforcement learning to enterprise problems?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for enterprises
items.answer:
I think it's a good idea in theory. But at the end of the day, RL is like a hammer. And you wanna be very, very clear on the problem you're using the hammer on, right?

So that's something, at least from my experience at Sierra, it's like you only know that when you're deep into the problem, right? Like, you need to have product knowledge, knowledge of everything that you can analyze the trajectories, all that. And that tells you where you need to do RL and all that.

What I'm trying to say is, you want to be using RL for the right things, but you also need to have the whole setup—the environment, all of that. And that requires a lot more work than the actual RL piece, right? That's just my take now.
